specAnchors.text: understand how a nucleus of U-235 can be split (the process of fission) by collision with a neutron and that this process releases energy as kinetic energy of the fission products
know that the fission of U-235 produces two radioactive daughter nuclei and a small number of neutrons

primer.text: Uranium-235 barely decays on its own, so reactors help it along: an absorbed neutron turns it into uranium-236, which splits at once. The split leaves two radioactive daughters, two or three fresh neutrons and gamma rays, with the released energy riding out as kinetic energy of the fragments.

modules.title: Spontaneous and induced fission
modules.opening: A large unstable nucleus can split into two smaller nuclei, but left alone it rarely does — that rare route is spontaneous fission. Normally the nucleus first absorbs a neutron, and the added instability makes it fall apart almost at once; that is induced fission, the route reactors rely on.
keyPoints: Fission splits one big unstable nucleus into a pair of smaller nuclei.
Uranium and plutonium isotopes are fissile, so they can be reactor fuels.
Spontaneous fission is rare; induced fission starts when the nucleus absorbs a neutron.
A U-235 nucleus that absorbs a neutron becomes uranium-236, which splits almost at once.
U-235's very long half-life means its own decay releases energy far too slowly.

low.restatement: Add a neutron to U-235 and you get U-236, which splits; without the added neutron, splits almost never happen.
low.analogy: A balanced stack of plates that barely wobbles on its own — nudge it with one more plate and it topples at once.
low.examPointer: Fissile is the key adjective for uranium and plutonium isotopes; use it when explaining why they are fuels.

medium.restatement: Capture of one neutron converts U-235 into the far less stable U-236; the 700-million-year half-life explains why the spontaneous route is negligible.
medium.analogy: A lazy river that never floods until one extra tributary arrives — then the dam bursts immediately.
medium.examPointer: Do not confuse spontaneous with induced: examiners award the contrast marks only when both routes are named correctly.

modules.title: Products and energy of fission
modules.opening: When induced fission splits a uranium-235 nucleus, the products are two radioactive daughter nuclei, two or three neutrons, and gamma rays — barium-144 and krypton-89 are one real pair. The daughters and neutrons fly apart fast because nuclear potential energy has become their kinetic energy, and power stations convert that into electrical energy.
keyPoints: Induced fission of U-235 produces two radioactive daughters, two or three neutrons, and gamma rays.
One actual split of U-235 makes barium-144 and krypton-89.
Energy stored as nuclear potential energy becomes kinetic energy of the fast products.
Nuclear power stations convert that kinetic energy into electrical energy.

low.restatement: One split: two radioactive daughters, two-to-three neutrons, gamma rays; the stored nuclear energy becomes their motion.
low.analogy: A wound-up spring toy snaps open: the stored tension (potential energy) turns into the pieces flying across the floor (kinetic energy).
low.examPointer: Balance fission equations exactly like decay equations — subtract products from the parent to find the missing piece.

medium.restatement: Product census per fission: 2 daughters + 2–3 neutrons + gamma rays; energy conservation moves nuclear potential energy into product kinetic energy.
medium.analogy: A plant pot cracking into two shards that skid across the patio — the crack releases the stress that was stored in the clay.
medium.examPointer: Daughters' names are not required in exams — balancing the numbers is; practise the subtraction method on plutonium and uranium cases.

glossary.definition: Describes isotopes, such as some of uranium and plutonium, that can undergo fission under the right conditions.
Fission started by the absorption of a neutron, making the nucleus unstable enough to split at once.
Fission that happens without extra energy added; rare in practice.
The two smaller radioactive nuclei produced when a parent nucleus splits.

workedExample.prompt: During a spontaneous fission reaction, plutonium-239 splits into palladium-112 and cadmium-124. What is emitted to balance the equation?
steps: Mass numbers: 239 − (112 + 124) = 3, so the missing mass number is 3.
Atomic numbers: 94 − (46 + 48) = 0, so the missing atomic number is 0.
A particle with mass number 1 and atomic number 0 is a neutron, and three of them give mass 3 with atomic 0.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Three neutrons (total mass number 3, atomic number 0) balance the equation.
